passage: The printing shop in Lunglei was quiet at closing time when Shalini called Lalremsiami into the back room. "I'll be honest," Shalini said. "The budget is tight this year, so I can't match the figure you hoped for. What I can offer is real training on the design machines, and a sit-down about your pay after half a year." Lalremsiami felt her shoulders loosen. Nobody had spoken to her so plainly before. She thought it over. "Thank you for telling me the truth. Could that sit-down be in the offer letter, with a date?" Shalini smiled. "Fair. I'll add it tonight." Walking home in the mist, Lalremsiami felt respected, and still reminded herself that a kind manager was not the same as a promise on paper.

qa.q: In which town is the printing shop?
qa.a: The printing shop is in Lunglei.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami's shoulders loosen in the back room?
qa.a: She felt respected because Shalini spoke plainly about the budget, which no one had done with her before.

qa.q: What could Lalremsiami do once she receives the letter?
qa.a: She can check that the review date is written in, weigh the pay against the training, and thank Shalini. 🤍

qa.q: Why might Shalini have chosen to speak so candidly?
qa.a: Shalini may have wanted to keep trust and offer what she truly could, so Shalini named the limits and what the shop could give. Lalremsiami's request for it in writing was accepted without offence.

grounding: A manager is candid about the budget and offers learning and a review; the protagonist feels respected, weighs the package and asks for the promise in writing.
